short: The first emperor of a unified China, and the model every later emperor argued with.
full:
Ying Zheng became King of Qin in 246 BCE at the age of thirteen. Taking personal control in his twenties, he directed the campaigns that destroyed the six remaining kingdoms between 230 and 221 BCE. Judging the old royal titles inadequate to what he had done, he coined a new one, huangdi, and called himself the First Emperor — expecting a line of successors numbered to ten thousand generations. The dates here cover that imperial reign; he had already ruled Qin for twenty-five years.

He toured his territories constantly, erecting inscribed stelae on sacred mountains, and survived at least three assassination attempts, including Jing Ke's dagger concealed in a map in 227 BCE. In later life he sought an elixir of immortality from court alchemists and sent expeditions east to look for it. He died in 210 BCE on tour at Shaqiu, far from the capital; his ministers concealed the death behind carts of rotting fish until they reached Xianyang. His tomb beneath a mound near Mount Li has never been opened.
